title: {{NAME}} and the Final That Lasted Forever
moral: Some moments are so full they stay with you your whole life.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a brilliant white hero soccer jersey with a golden unicorn emblem, white shorts, and gold-white cleats — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The Hero Football Championship was played once every four years.

For most heroes, it was the match of their careers.

For {{NAME}}, it was his first.

He was the youngest player ever selected for the championship squad, on the recommendation of two people: the team's tactical analyst and Solari, a unicorn who had been watching the junior leagues for three years and had walked into the selection committee's office one morning and indicated, clearly, that she had a recommendation.

The selection committee had, after some discussion, accepted it.

pages.content:
Solari worked with {{NAME}} in the weeks before the final.

She didn't coach exactly. She watched, and sometimes touched her horn to his shoulder before a training session, and for ten minutes afterward, everything he did was clearer than usual: he could see the whole pitch, read the movements before they happened, feel the game's rhythm as something almost musical.

"What does that feel like when it fades?" his teammate asked once.

"Like coming back from somewhere very clear," said {{NAME}}. "And knowing I was there once. And knowing I can find it again."

pages.content:
Championship day: ninety thousand people in the stadium.

{{NAME}} had never played in front of more than two thousand.

He stood at the centre circle before kick-off and felt the crowd noise as a physical weight.

Solari was at the touchline. She touched her horn briefly to the wall.

He felt it from sixty metres: the clarity arriving, quieting the crowd noise, showing him the pitch as it actually was.

He breathed out.

"There," he said, to no one. "Found it."

pages.content:
He played the best match of his life.

Not because he scored. He scored once, late, but the goal that won it was someone else's, an assist he had set up with a pass that found space nobody else had seen.

But he was everywhere the ball needed to go.

The tactical analyst said afterward: "I've watched football for thirty years. That was complete."

Solari was waiting for him outside the stadium.

He put his forehead briefly against hers.

"Thank you," he said.

pages.content:
Walking home in the late evening, medal around his neck, he thought about the clarity.

Not Solari's horn: he could find it without that now. She had shown him where it lived and how to get there.

He had it on his own tonight in the second half. All of it, without the touch.

In bed, medal on the pillow, he lay in the dark and thought: that's who I am when I'm exactly myself.

He fell asleep still feeling it.

Somewhere in the park, Solari stood under the stars, and her horn was very bright.
